# Canton Hyland

> Canton Hyland Hardware (Group) Co., Ltd. manufactures architectural door hardware in Guangdong, China — panic
> exit devices, mortise lock cases, lever handles, door closers, hinges and bathroom
> accessories — and exports to distributors and project buyers in over thirty markets.

This site is a product and company reference. Orders are not placed here: enquiries
go to the export team by email, or through the company's Alibaba storefront.

## Key facts

- Manufacturer, not a trading company. Operating since 1998.
- 523 published models across 15 categories.
- Quality management certified to ISO 9001.
- Test reports are published per model, not per range — see the download centre.

## Product categories

- [Panic Exit Devices](https://cantonlock.com/products/panic-exit-devices/): Push bars and touch bars for escape routes, including fire-door, alarmed, double-door and two-point locking versions. 46 models.
- [Night Latches & Rim Locks](https://cantonlock.com/products/night-latches-rim-locks/): Surface-mounted night latches and rim locks, most with a 60mm backset, fitted through a single cylinder hole in an existing door. 25 models.
- [Stainless Steel Handles](https://cantonlock.com/products/stainless-steel-handles/): Stainless steel lever handles, including the 9000 series for doors of 35–50mm, and a concealed sliding-door handle. 43 models.
- [Lever Handles](https://cantonlock.com/products/lever-handles/): Tubular lever handle sets, mostly zinc alloy, for entrance, privacy and passage doors, with a 60/70mm backset and keying alike with deadbolts. 50 models.
- [Knob Locks](https://cantonlock.com/products/knob-locks/): Cylindrical and tubular knob locks for entry, privacy, passage and communication functions. 59 models.
- [Bathroom Accessories](https://cantonlock.com/products/bathroom-accessories/): Bathroom accessories, most of them published in stainless steel. 54 models.
- [Brass & Steel Door Hinges](https://cantonlock.com/products/brass-steel-hinges/): Brass, stainless-steel and steel hinge ranges for architectural door applications. 29 models.
- [Deadbolts](https://cantonlock.com/products/deadbolts/): Single- and double-cylinder deadbolts with a 25mm throw, an anti-saw roller insert and a 60/70mm adjustable backset. 11 models.
- [Door Closers](https://cantonlock.com/products/door-closers/): Door closers with aluminium bodies for commercial doors, plus a floor hinge for timber doors. 7 models.
- [Grip Handle Sets](https://cantonlock.com/products/grip-handle-sets/): Grip, pull and concealed handle sets for entrance and sliding doors. 14 models.
- [Glass Door Accessories](https://cantonlock.com/products/glass-door-accessories/): Patch fittings and pull handles for frameless glass-door assemblies. 23 models.
- [Hardware Accessories](https://cantonlock.com/products/hardware-accessories/): Door viewers, stoppers, transfer devices, bolts, indicators, latches and guards. 62 models.
- [Lock Cases](https://cantonlock.com/products/lock-cases/): Mortise lock cases in multiple backset, centre-distance and bolt configurations. 52 models.
- [Lock Cylinders](https://cantonlock.com/products/lock-cylinders/): Profile and keyed cylinders, including master-key system applications. 45 models.
- [Sliding Hook Locks](https://cantonlock.com/products/sliding-hook-locks/): Hook-lock hardware for sliding doors and narrow-stile applications. 3 models.

## Guides and articles

### Buying guides — dimension charts, code cross-references and selection

- [Cylindrical and Tubular Lock Comparison 2026: Four Families, Every Series, and What Heavy Duty Actually Changes](https://cantonlock.com/guides/cylindrical-and-tubular-lock-comparison-2026/): 59 knob and lever locks for bored doors, in four families: tubular, light-duty cylindrical, heavy-duty cylindrical and commercial. Side by side from their specification rows, with the one row that does not separate them, and the rows that do.
- [Exit Device Comparison 2026: Every Push Bar in the Range by Length, Latching and Door](https://cantonlock.com/guides/exit-device-comparison-2026/): 46 records sit in our panic exit device family, and only 27 of them are exit devices. Here they are in three tables (single doors, pairs, special purposes) built from their specification rows, with the missing rows and the conflicting ones named.
- [Mortise Lock Case Comparison 2026: Every Published Backset and Center Distance, Side by Side](https://cantonlock.com/guides/mortise-lock-case-comparison-2026/): 27 of our mortise lock cases publish both a backset and a center distance. Here they are in two tables, narrow-stile and standard, with the naming traps and the gaps stated plainly.
- [Backset and Door Thickness Chart 2026: What 589 Published Models Actually Take](https://cantonlock.com/guides/backset-door-thickness-chart-2026/): Two numbers decide whether a replacement lock drops into a door that is already machined: the backset and the door thickness range. This is what our published catalog actually carries (counted from the records rather than quoted from a brochure) with the imperial equivalents, the measuring method, and the one dimension that is not a backset and gets confused with it.
- [Brass Hardware 2026: Which Brass, Why Lead Is In It, and the One Failure Mode That Decides Coastal Projects](https://cantonlock.com/guides/brass-alloys-and-dezincification-2026/): "Solid brass" names a family of alloys that behave differently, and the difference that matters most is whether the alloy resists dezincification. This page sets out the brasses used in door hardware, explains why lead is in most of them and what the low-lead alternatives cost, describes dezincification and where DZR brass is genuinely required, separates brass from bronze, and counts what our own catalog publishes.
- [Validating a Hardware Certificate 2026: The Seven Parts, DoP and CE Marking, and the Six Red Flags](https://cantonlock.com/guides/certification-and-test-validation-2026/): A certificate either survives being checked or it does not, and checking one takes about five minutes if you know what to look at. This page sets out the seven parts every genuine test certificate carries, explains the difference between accreditation and certification, covers Declarations of Performance and CE marking for door hardware, lists the six red flags that mean stop, and states plainly what we do and do not hold.
- [Chrome, Satin Chrome and Satin Nickel 2026: Why Two Suppliers' "Polished Chrome" Do Not Match, and How to Specify One That Does](https://cantonlock.com/guides/chrome-finish-differences-2026/): Chrome is a thin top layer over nickel, which is why nickel decides how it looks and how long it lasts. This page explains the plating stack, separates polished chrome from satin chrome from satin nickel by the property that actually distinguishes them, gives the codes, and shows from our own 336 finish rows why a finish written as a name rather than a code cannot be reordered.
- [Lock Function Selection 2026: A Decision Table by Room Type, and the Two Questions That Settle Every Opening](https://cantonlock.com/guides/commercial-lock-function-decision-2026/): Choosing a lock function is not a catalog problem, it is a two-question problem: who is allowed through, and what happens to the person already inside. This page turns that into a decision table covering the room types a commercial building actually contains, names the three function errors that create life-safety problems rather than inconvenience, and states how many models of each function our own catalog carries.
- [Container Loading for Door Hardware 2026: Why a 40HQ Does Not Hold More Than a 40GP](https://cantonlock.com/guides/container-loading-door-hardware-2026/): Door hardware is a weight-limited cargo, not a volume-limited one. Worked from our own shipping worksheet: the median carton density is 614 kg per cubic meter, which is above the point where a 40-foot container runs out of payload before it runs out of space. The high cube buys 15 per cent more volume and, for this cargo, no more hardware.
- [Corrosion Resistance 2026: EN 1670 Grades 0–5, Salt Spray Hours, and What the Test Does Not Tell You](https://cantonlock.com/guides/corrosion-resistance-en-1670-2026/): EN 1670 grades door hardware corrosion resistance from 0 to 5, and each grade is a number of hours in a neutral salt spray cabinet. This page gives the hours for every grade, explains what ASTM B117 and ANSI/BHMA A156.18 do on the other side of the Atlantic, names the three environments where a grade chosen by habit fails, and is honest about what a cabinet test cannot predict.
- [200,000 Cycles: What a Durability Figure Means in EN 1906 and in ANSI/BHMA, and Why It Is Not the Same Number](https://cantonlock.com/guides/cycle-testing-durability-grades-2026/): We publish 200,000 cycles on 132 models. In EN 1906 that is the top durability category. In ANSI/BHMA A156.2 it is the entry grade. Both statements are true, and a specification that reads one as the other will either over-buy or under-buy. This page sets out what a cycle test actually is, what each scale asks for, and where our own figure sits on both.
- [Dimensional Interchangeability 2026: The Seven Dimensions That Decide Whether a Lock Drops In, and How Many We Publish](https://cantonlock.com/guides/dimensional-interchangeability-2026/): "Is it interchangeable?" is answered by seven dimensions, and two of them are the ones almost nobody publishes. This page lists them in the order they cause failures, explains why matching the backset is not enough, sets out what to send a factory when you want a drop-in for a discontinued lock, and counts how many of our own 257 lock products publish each dimension, including the one at two per cent.
- [Door Closer Mounting 2026: Regular Arm, Top Jamb, Parallel Arm and Slide Track Compared](https://cantonlock.com/guides/door-closer-mounting-positions-2026/): The same door closer performs differently depending on where it is mounted, and the mounting is usually chosen on site by whoever is holding the drill. This page compares the four standard arrangements on the three things that matter (mechanical efficiency, projection into the opening, and vulnerability) explains why a parallel arm can cost you a power size, and sets out which side of the door each one lives on.
- [Door Closer Power Size 2026: EN 1154 Sizes 1–7, A156.4, and How to Pick One from the Door](https://cantonlock.com/guides/door-closer-power-size-2026/): A door closer is specified by a power size, and the power size is derived from the door (its leaf width and its mass) not from the opening or the building type. This page sets out the EN 1154 size ladder with the leaf widths each covers, how the ANSI/BHMA A156.4 approach differs, the three adjustments that are not the power size, and the accessibility constraint that overrides all of it.
- [Door Hardware HS Codes 2026: Headings 8301 and 8302 Decoded, and Where the Six Digits Stop](https://cantonlock.com/guides/door-hardware-hs-codes-2026/): Almost every product in a door hardware catalog classifies under one of two HS headings: 8301 for locks and keys, 8302 for mountings and fittings. This page sets out the subheadings under each, names the four that are most often got wrong (door closers, keys shipped separately, parts, and furniture versus building fittings) and explains exactly where the internationally agreed code ends and your own country's begins.
- [Door Preparation 2026: The 161 Bore, the 86 Mortise Pocket, and What "Prepped For" Actually Guarantees](https://cantonlock.com/guides/door-preparation-161-and-86-2026/): A door arrives on site "prepped", and whether the lock fits is decided by holes cut weeks earlier in another factory. This page sets out the standard bored-lock and mortise-lock preparations with their dimensions, explains the ANSI/BHMA A115 series that governs them, and lists the five things a purchase order has to say before a door manufacturer can cut anything.
- [Door Thickness to Cylinder Length 2026: The Arithmetic, a Lookup Table, and Why the Answer Is Often Rounded Up](https://cantonlock.com/guides/door-thickness-to-cylinder-length-2026/): Sizing a euro cylinder is one subtraction and one rounding, and the rounding is where it goes wrong. This page gives the calculation, a door-thickness lookup table worked against the nine lengths we actually publish, explains why a thin door still gets a protruding cylinder, and shows what changes when the lock case is not centered in the leaf.
- [EN 1125 or EN 179 in 2026: Panic Bar or Emergency Lever, and the One Question About People That Decides It](https://cantonlock.com/guides/en-1125-vs-en-179-2026/): Two European standards cover escape hardware and they are chosen by who uses the building, not by how important the door is. This page explains what separates EN 1125 from EN 179, gives the occupancy test that decides between them, decodes the classification digits, lists the three mistakes that produce a non-compliant opening, and states what our own exit range does and does not hold.
- [EN to ANSI/BHMA Cross-Reference 2026: What Maps, What Does Not, and Why](https://cantonlock.com/guides/en-ansi-bhma-cross-reference-2026/): Specifiers ask for a conversion table between EN and ANSI/BHMA door hardware standards. What exists is a scope map, not an equivalence: the two systems classify different properties, and a product certified to one carries no automatic claim under the other. This page sets out which standard covers which product family on each side, what each one measures, and the four places the mapping genuinely breaks.
- [Euro Cylinder Size Chart 2026: Every Length and Split, and How to Measure Yours](https://cantonlock.com/guides/euro-cylinder-size-chart-2026/): A euro cylinder is described by two numbers, and getting them the wrong way round is the commonest ordering error in door hardware. This is the full size chart to EN 1303 and DIN 18252 geometry, the nine overall lengths we publish, the split combinations that add up to each one, and the measurement that decides which you need.
- [Exit Device Outside Trim 2026: Every Trim Function Compared, Dogging Rules, and Why the Bar Is Never the Decision](https://cantonlock.com/guides/exit-device-outside-trim-functions-2026/): An exit device has two halves and only one of them is a decision. The bar inside always lets people out; the trim outside decides who gets in, whether the door can be held unlocked during business hours, and whether the opening still complies in a fire. This page compares every outside trim function, sets out the dogging rules including the one that is absolute on fire doors, and counts how many of our own fifteen trims publish their function.
- [Finish Code Reference 2026: The 23 Codes, the BHMA Numbers, and the Four Pairs That Reverse](https://cantonlock.com/guides/finish-code-reference-2026/): A finish code on a purchase order decides what arrives, and four pairs of codes in common use are reversals of each other. This is the reference: the 23 codes our catalog uses, how they line up with BHMA 600-series and US26x numbers, the pairs that get transposed, and a count of how inconsistently our own catalog spells them.
- [Fire Door Hardware 2026: Which Components Must Be Rated, EN 1634-1 vs UL 10C and NFPA 252, and What a Certificate Covers](https://cantonlock.com/guides/fire-door-hardware-what-must-be-rated-2026/): A fire door is not a product; it is a tested assembly, and every item fixed to it is part of what was tested. This page lists the components that must be rated, explains the difference between EN 1634-1 and UL 10C / NFPA 252 including the hose stream test that only one of them has, sets out what a certificate actually covers, and states plainly which of our own products do and do not carry a fire rating today.
- [Glass Door Hardware 2026: Thickness Ranges, Cut-Out Dimensions, and the One Step That Cannot Be Undone](https://cantonlock.com/guides/glass-door-thickness-and-cutouts-2026/): Glass door hardware is the only category where getting the sequence wrong destroys the door rather than delaying it. This page gives the glass thickness ranges our fittings actually accept, explains the glass gap dimension and the corner radius on a cut-out, sets out why every hole must be made before toughening, and lists what has to be on the glass shop drawing before anybody orders anything.
- [Door Hardware Refurbishment Survey 2026: The Fourteen Fields, What Needs a Screwdriver, and How to Sample a Building You Cannot Fully Open](https://cantonlock.com/guides/hardware-refurbishment-survey-2026/): On a refurbishment the drawings are a record of what was intended, not of what is on the doors. This page gives the fourteen fields worth recording per leaf, separates the ones you can capture from the corridor from the ones that need a screwdriver, sets out a sampling rule by door type, and shows how the survey becomes an order.
- [Door Hardware Warranty 2026: What "Ten Year" Actually Covers, the Five Exclusions That Do the Work, and How to Make a Claim Succeed](https://cantonlock.com/guides/hardware-warranty-what-it-covers-2026/): A warranty is read as a number of years and decided by its exclusions. This page separates warranty from guarantee from statutory rights, lists the five exclusions that defeat most claims, explains why installation and cleaning are where liability actually lands, sets out what a claim needs to succeed, and says what a factory can honestly promise about a part it will never see again.
- [Hinge Grades and Hinge Count 2026: EN 1935 Grades 1–14, ANSI/BHMA A156.1, and How Many a Door Needs](https://cantonlock.com/guides/hinge-grades-and-count-2026/): Two questions decide a hinge specification: what grade, and how many. EN 1935 answers the first with grades 1 to 14 tied to a tested door mass; ANSI/BHMA A156.1 answers it with a weight class and a frequency. Neither answers the second, which is governed by leaf height and mass. This page sets out both ladders, the count rule, and the three failure modes that come from getting the count right and the grade wrong.
- [Key Blanks and Restricted Profiles 2026: Open, Restricted and Patented Keyways, and What Key Control Actually Buys](https://cantonlock.com/guides/key-blanks-and-restricted-profiles-2026/): A key that enters a lock and a key that turns it are two different achievements, and the difference is the keyway. This page explains what a blank and a profile are, separates open from restricted from patented keyways, is precise about what each one stops and what it does not, explains why a patent expiring changes the security of a building that was specified years earlier, and lists what a buyer has to decide before a master key system can be cut.
- [Lever Return and EN 1906 2026: Why a Lever Must Curve Back, and What the Eight-Digit Classification Says](https://cantonlock.com/guides/lever-return-and-en-1906-2026/): A straight lever handle looks cleaner than a returned one and is rejected on most commercial specifications, for a reason that has nothing to do with taste. This page explains what lever return is, the safety and accessibility requirements behind it, why a knob fails accessibility where a lever passes, and how to read the eight fields of an EN 1906 handle classification instead of quoting only the first one.
- [Master Key Hierarchy Planning 2026: The Levels, What Cross-Keying Really Costs, and How to Leave Room for the Building You Will Have](https://cantonlock.com/guides/master-key-hierarchy-planning-2026/): A master key system is designed once and lived with for twenty years, and almost every system that runs out of room ran out for the same two reasons: too many levels for the building, and cross-keying granted door by door as favors. This page sets out the hierarchy, explains why every master level and every cross-key consumes capacity from a finite pool, and gives the questions to answer before a single cylinder is cut.
- [Material Traceability 2026: EN 10204 Types 2.1, 2.2, 3.1 and 3.2, Heat Numbers, and What a Hardware Factory Can Honestly Trace](https://cantonlock.com/guides/material-traceability-mill-certs-2026/): "Send the material certificate" means four different documents, and the difference between them is who signed it and whether the test was on your metal. This page sets out the EN 10204 document types, explains heat numbers and where the chain of custody genuinely breaks in small hardware, separates material traceability from RoHS and REACH compliance, and says which of these a door hardware factory can honestly provide.
- [MOQ, Tooling and Lead Time 2026: What Actually Sets the Minimum, and Why 300 and 5,000 Are Both True](https://cantonlock.com/guides/moq-tooling-and-lead-time-2026/): A buyer asks for a minimum order quantity and gets a range, which reads as evasion and is not. This page explains the four things that actually set an MOQ (the finish batch, the tooling, the packaging and the model's own production run) why our published range runs from 300 to 5,000 pieces, what the 30-day lead time is actually counting, and the three decisions a buyer can make that move all of these in their favor.
- [Powder Coating and RAL 2026: Why a Color Number Does Not Specify a Finish, What Pretreatment Decides, and What to Write on the Order](https://cantonlock.com/guides/powder-coating-and-ral-2026/): A RAL number names a color and nothing else, not gloss, not texture, not process, not durability. This page explains what RAL specifies and what it leaves open, why pretreatment decides whether a coating survives, where powder coating fails on hardware geometry, which tests are worth citing, and the four lines that make a finish orderable.
- [Qualifying a Hardware Supplier 2026: Factory, Trader or Broker, the Five Questions That Separate Them, and What to Verify](https://cantonlock.com/guides/qualifying-a-hardware-supplier-2026/): Three kinds of company answer a hardware inquiry and all three will say yes. This page explains what a factory, a trading company and a broker each actually control, gives five questions whose answers separate them without anybody having to be confronted, lists what can be verified independently, and applies the whole test to us.
- [Samples and Incoming Inspection 2026: The Golden Sample, What to Measure, and What a Sample Cannot Tell You](https://cantonlock.com/guides/samples-and-incoming-inspection-2026/): A sample is the cheapest place to discover that a supplier understood something differently from how you meant it. This page sets out the three kinds of sample and which one to ask for, the golden sample procedure that makes a sample enforceable instead of decorative, exactly what to measure when one arrives, the three properties a sample genuinely cannot demonstrate, and how to write an inspection standard that a third-party inspector can apply without calling you.
- [Writing Door Hardware Section 08 71 00 in 2026: The Three Parts, What Belongs in Each, and the Clauses That Cost Money](https://cantonlock.com/guides/specification-section-08-71-00-2026/): A door hardware specification is a three-part document with a fixed shape, and most of the money lost on a hardware package is lost by putting the right sentence in the wrong part. This page sets out what belongs in Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3, shows how a hardware set is written so a factory can quote it without a phone call, and names the four clauses that quietly decide the price.
- [Door Handle Spindle Sizes 2026: 8mm and 9mm Squares, Split Spindles, and How to Calculate the Length](https://cantonlock.com/guides/spindle-sizes-and-length-2026/): The spindle is the cheapest part of a door handle set and the one that most often makes a shipment unusable. Three numbers decide whether a handle will turn a lock: the square size, the spindle length, and whether the spindle is solid or split. This page sets out all three, gives the length formula, and shows what our own catalog actually publishes.
- [Stainless Grade Selection 2026: 201 vs 304 vs 316, What Each Costs, and Why "304/201" on a Spec Sheet Is the Real Problem](https://cantonlock.com/guides/stainless-grade-selection-201-304-316-2026/): 201, 304 and 316 look identical in the hand and behave very differently on a building. This page sets out what separates them chemically, where each belongs, what the cost difference actually is, and then does the uncomfortable part, counts how many of our own 313 stainless products name a grade at all, and explains why a specification that says "304/201" has answered nothing.
- [Strike Plates and Keeps 2026: ANSI Strike vs T-Strike, Lip Length, and the Dimension Nobody Measures](https://cantonlock.com/guides/strike-plates-and-keeps-2026/): The strike is the cheapest component in a door opening and the one that decides whether the lock ever latches properly. This page sets out the two standard North American strike sizes, the European keep conventions, how to work out lip length instead of guessing it, the difference between square and radius corners, and why a security upgrade that stops at the lock has upgraded nothing.
- [Door Hardware Submittal Package 2026: Every Document the Reviewer Needs, and the Four That Get It Rejected](https://cantonlock.com/guides/submittal-package-contents-2026/): A hardware submittal is rejected for the same handful of reasons on almost every project, and none of them is the hardware. This page lists what a complete package contains, names the four omissions that send it back, explains the difference between a product datasheet and evidence, sets out who signs what, and states plainly which of these documents we publish, which we supply on request, and which we do not have at all.
- [Door Hardware Drawings 2026: PDF, DWG, STEP and BIM Compared, and What a Factory Can Actually Give You](https://cantonlock.com/guides/technical-drawings-what-to-expect-2026/): Asking a hardware factory for "the CAD" produces a different file in every country, and half the time the file you get cannot do the job you wanted it for. This page separates the three kinds of drawing that answer three different questions, compares the formats and what each one is really for, explains why a 3D solid often does not exist even at a competent factory, and states our own drawing coverage as a number rather than a promise.
- [Universal or Handed 2026: Which Hardware Is Reversible, Which Is Not, and the Four Products That Catch Projects Out](https://cantonlock.com/guides/universal-vs-handed-hardware-2026/): "Universal" means three different things in a hardware catalog and only one of them means you can stop thinking about handing. This page separates non-handed from field-reversible from factory-handed, names the four products that are handed when people assume they are not, explains what reversing actually does inside a lock, and gives the line to put on an order so the question never arrives.
- [Zinc Alloy Hardware 2026: What Zamak Actually Is, Where It Belongs, and the Four Ways a Bad Casting Fails](https://cantonlock.com/guides/zinc-alloy-die-cast-hardware-2026/): Zinc alloy is the second most common material in our catalog and the one buyers are most suspicious of, usually for reasons that describe bad castings rather than the material. This page explains what zamak is, what die casting is genuinely good at, the four distinct ways a poor zinc part fails, where zinc should never be used at all, and what to ask a factory so the answer means something.

### News and insights — short answers to specific questions

- [A Brass Piano Hinge Is Usually Not Brass](https://cantonlock.com/news/brass-piano-hinge-is-a-finish-not-a-metal/): In this trade "brass piano hinge" almost always names the finish, not the metal. Ours is iron under a matt black or polished brass finish, in 1", 1-1/4", 2" and 3" widths, and our own catalog claimed stainless steel until 16 September, which is a good illustration of how the confusion survives.
- [Entrance, Privacy, Passage: Choosing Between Twelve Cylindrical Locks](https://cantonlock.com/news/choosing-a-cylindrical-lock-entrance-privacy-passage/): 587, 607, 5807, 5870, 592, 598, 575, 578, 9210, 595, 609 and 5831 look like twelve choices and are mostly one choice made twelve times. Nearly all of them take a 60/70mm adjustable backset and a 35–45mm (1-3/8" to 1-3/4") door, so the decision is function first, chassis second, and one of the twelve goes to a 90mm (3-9/16") backset when the others stop at 70.
- [A 25mm Throw and a Collar That Spins: Deadbolts D101 and D102](https://cantonlock.com/news/deadbolt-d101-d102-and-the-rim-alternative/): A deadbolt does one job the latch above it cannot: it throws a solid bolt that no card and no shim will move. Ours throw 25mm (1"), in zinc die-cast with a hardened steel roller pin against sawing, on a five-pin solid brass cylinder, and the free-turning collar is the detail that matters most and photographs least.
- [45 to 90: Reading Our Euro Cylinder Range](https://cantonlock.com/news/euro-cylinder-range-45-to-90/): In this range the model number is the overall length in millimeters, so 45, 54, 60, 70, 80 and 90 are six lengths rather than six products. All are solid brass. What the letters after the number mean is partly documented and partly not, and this article says which is which.
- [650 to 1110mm: Which Push Bar Length Your Door Takes](https://cantonlock.com/news/exit-device-push-bar-length/): Bar length is the dimension most often left off an exit-device inquiry, and the one that cannot be corrected on site. Our published lengths run 650, 800, 900, 1000, 1040, 1050 and 1110mm (43-11/16"), some adjustable and some not, and which of those your door takes is decided by the leaf width rather than by the model you liked.
- [US26D, 626, 630: A Finish Code Is Not a Color](https://cantonlock.com/news/finish-codes-us26d-626-630/): A North American specification writes 626, not "satin chrome". The number encodes the base metal as well as the appearance, so 626 and 652 are the same color and different products. Of 519 published Canton Hyland records, 77 can be given a number honestly; the other 442 cannot, and each has a reason.
- [200,000 Cycles: What the LH Lever Range Is Actually Rated For](https://cantonlock.com/news/lever-handle-range-lh852-lh853-lh855/): LH852, LH853, LH855, 808 and 6491 share a published cycle life of 200,000 operations, a 60/70mm backset, a 35–45mm (1-3/8" to 1-3/4") adjustable door thickness and a solid steel zinc-plated chassis behind a zinc-alloy lever. What separates them is the function set and the shape, and only one of the five offers a dummy.
- [Occupied or Vacant: What a Washroom Indicator Actually Has to Do](https://cantonlock.com/news/occupied-vacant-washroom-indicator-bolt/): An indicator bolt is a lock and a sign in one part, and the sign is the half that gets specified badly. It has to be readable from standing distance, it has to be releasable from outside in an emergency, and on a public washroom it has to survive being operated several hundred times a day by people who are not being careful.
- [The Rim Night Latch: What 564 and 1073 Actually Measure](https://cantonlock.com/news/rim-night-latch-564-and-1073/): A rim night latch sits on the face of the door rather than inside it, which changes every dimension that matters: backset, door thickness range, latch extension and deadbolt throw. The 564 and the 1073 answer the same job in two different metals, and the difference between single-side and double-side is a security decision rather than a convenience one.
- [Lever Length, Rose Diameter, Projection: The Stainless 9000 Levers](https://cantonlock.com/news/stainless-lever-range-9007-9008-9014/): The 9014, 9007 and 9008 are stainless lever sets on a 53mm (2-1/16") rose for a 35–50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16") door. The 9014 publishes a 135mm (5-5/16") lever, 60mm (2-3/8") projection and a 9mm (3/8") rose; the 9007 a 132mm (5-3/16") lever, 63mm (2-1/2") projection and an 8mm (5/16") rose. The 9008 publishes six rows in total, and this article says so rather than filling the gap in.
- [UL 305 Is a Listing, Not a Grade](https://cantonlock.com/news/ul-305-is-a-listing-not-a-grade/): EN 1125 is a standard you test against. ANSI/BHMA A156.3 is a standard that grades you 1, 2 or 3. UL 305 is neither, it is the basis for a listing, which is an ongoing arrangement with a certification body rather than a document you hold. Confusing the three is how a compliant-looking device fails a submittal.
- [A Padlock Chained to a Knight in Germany](https://cantonlock.com/news/what-an-old-padlock-tells-a-lock-factory/): Our principal found it on a German street, chained around the ankles of a cast-iron knight outside a hotel, and photographed it because the older a thing is the more it draws you in. We cannot tell you who made it or when, rust removes exactly the evidence that would answer that. We can tell you what is still legible in the metal, which is more than you would expect, and why we are not going to invent the rest.
- [Fitting a Euro Cylinder: Five Steps, and the Two Everyone Skips](https://cantonlock.com/news/fitting-a-euro-cylinder/): A euro cylinder goes in and out through the lock case, held by one screw, and the whole job takes two minutes once the cylinder is the right length. Almost every failed fitting is one of two things: the cam was not turned before it was pushed through, or nobody tried the key with the door shut.
- [Why the Catalog Is This Wide: 28 Years of Cutting Moulds for Other People's Doors](https://cantonlock.com/news/why-the-catalogue-is-this-wide/): Almost nothing in this range was designed by us in the abstract. A buyer somewhere could not find a part in their own market, brought us a drawing or a sample, and we cut the mould. Do that since 1998 and the catalog ends up looking like a map of other people's doors.
- [Why a Double Fire Door Needs a Coordinator, and How to Size One](https://cantonlock.com/news/door-coordinator-double-fire-door/): A pair of fire doors with two closers will close in whichever order the springs decide. If the active leaf arrives first, the astragal holds it open and the door does not latch, so the assembly is no longer a fire door. A coordinator forces the order. This is what it has to match to work.
- [Five Months of Tooling: How the 311 Exit Device Was Made](https://cantonlock.com/news/what-it-takes-to-tool-a-new-exit-device/): A customer called at eleven at night asking for a price, came to the factory the next afternoon with a sample, and asked whether we could make it. Three moulds, three toolmakers, one pause of over a year, and five months of trial-and-correction later, the 311 existed. This is what buying a custom exit device actually costs a factory, and why a lead time on a tooled product is not the same number as a lead time on a catalog one.
- [Which Exit Device Standard Your Project Is Actually Under](https://cantonlock.com/news/en-1125-or-ansi-which-standard-your-project-needs/): EN 1125 and ANSI/BHMA A156.3 are not two grades of the same thing. They come from different building codes, measure different failures, and a device built to one is not automatically acceptable under the other. The standard is decided by where the door is, not by what you prefer.
- [How Many Levels Your Master Key System Actually Needs](https://cantonlock.com/news/master-key-systems-how-many-levels-you-need/): A master key system is a hierarchy, and the number of levels in it is a decision about who is allowed through which door, not a hardware specification. We build to five levels, GGMK down to the change key, with four tiers of management keying above the individual lock. Most buildings need three.
- [Cross-Referencing a Lock You Already Buy](https://cantonlock.com/news/cross-referencing-a-lock-you-already-buy/): A lot of the searches that reach us are somebody else's model number, another factory's rim lock, another brand's hinge, a part code off an old invoice. They are all the same question: what do I order to get this again. Six dimensions decide the answer, and the model number is not one of them.
- [DS013 and DS011 Are Not the Same Kind of Thing](https://cantonlock.com/news/door-stop-holder-or-flush-bolt/): Somebody searched "door stopper ds013 vs ds011" and landed on us. It is a fair question and the answer is that only one of them is a door stopper, DS011 is a flush bolt, which does the opposite job. Here is how to tell three commonly confused items apart before they are on the order.
- [Cutsheets, CAD and BIM: What We Have and What We Do Not](https://cantonlock.com/news/what-documents-you-can-actually-get/): People arrive here searching for a cutsheet, a DWG, a BIM object or a ficha técnica. Some of that we publish today, some of it we can send on request, and one of it does not exist yet. Saying which is which is more useful than a download page that promises everything.
- [70 Is the Total, Not the Split](https://cantonlock.com/news/euro-cylinder-length-and-split/): The number in 70SN is the overall length of the cylinder in millimeters. It says nothing about how that 70mm (2-3/4") is divided either side of the cam, and the division is the part that decides whether the key turns once the door is hung.
- [A Test Report Covers a Model, Not a Range](https://cantonlock.com/news/what-a-test-report-actually-covers/): Our EN 1125 report covers one exit device: KD070/30-290. Our durability report covers one lock: 607 SS ET. Neither covers the family it sits in, and a supplier who lets you believe otherwise has handed you a problem that surfaces at handover.
- [What OEM Actually Changes, and What It Does Not](https://cantonlock.com/news/what-oem-actually-changes/): Putting your brand on a lock is four separate decisions, not one, and only one of them costs real money. Three of them change nothing about the part. The fourth is the one that needs a mould.
- [Handing: The One-Letter Answer That Holds Up Orders](https://cantonlock.com/news/handing-left-right-and-universal/): Left, right or universal is a single character on an order line and the most common reason a quotation goes back for clarification. It is decided by where the hinges are and which way the door opens, and the two conventions in use disagree with each other.
- [The Six Values a Hardware Order Actually Needs](https://cantonlock.com/news/six-values-an-order-needs/): Most inquiries arrive with a model number and a quantity, and most of those go back with a question. Six values decide whether a part can be installed, and an inquiry carrying all six can be quoted the same day.
- [Trim Handle or Panic Bar: What the Outside of a Fire Exit Door Needs](https://cantonlock.com/news/trim-handle-or-panic-bar/): A panic bar opens the door from inside. It does nothing for the person outside. The part that lets them in is a separate order line, and getting the two confused is the most common way an exit-door schedule arrives incomplete.
- [ANSI Grade 1 or EN 1125: Which Standard Your Exit Device Has to Meet](https://cantonlock.com/news/ansi-grade-1-vs-en-1125-exit-devices/): They are not two grades of the same thing. ANSI/BHMA A156.3 rates an exit device by cycles and force; EN 1125 tests whether a panicking crowd can get out. Which one you need is decided by the country your building is in, not by which sounds stronger.
- [Why Aluminum Doors Drop, and What the Lock Case Has to Do With It](https://cantonlock.com/news/narrow-stile-aluminium-door-lock-sag/): A narrow-stile aluminum door that no longer latches has almost never got a broken lock. It has dropped a few millimeters at the far edge, and the lock is simply the first place anyone notices. Here is what actually moves, and which of it is a hardware decision.
- [Push Bar or Touch Bar: Which Panic Device Your Door Needs](https://cantonlock.com/news/push-bar-or-touch-bar-panic-exit-devices/): A push bar pivots and travels; a touch bar depresses flush into its own housing. They cost differently, they fail differently, and only one of them survives a corridor that gets hit by trolleys. Canton Hyland builds the push-bar type across all 42 devices in the range.
- [304, 201 or 316: Which Stainless Steel You Are Actually Buying](https://cantonlock.com/news/stainless-steel-grades-304-201-316/): Three grades look identical in a photograph, cost differently, and behave nothing alike within sight of the sea. 201 substitutes manganese for nickel and rusts where 304 does not; 316 adds molybdenum and survives where 304 pits. Here is how to tell which one you have been quoted.
- [What One Frameless Glass Door Actually Needs](https://cantonlock.com/news/what-a-frameless-glass-door-needs/): A frameless glass door is not a product, it is an assembly of six or seven parts ordered from three different categories. Buyers quote the handle, forget the floor spring, and discover the over-panel patch on site. Here is the whole list, in the order it gets forgotten.
- [The Door Schedule: How Hardware Is Actually Specified](https://cantonlock.com/news/door-hardware-schedule-guide/): Projects do not buy locks. They buy door types, and each door type is a set of hardware that has to agree with itself. The document that decides this is the door schedule, and it is worth understanding before you quote against one.
- [Backset and Center Distance: How to Read a Mortise Lock Case Number](https://cantonlock.com/news/mortise-lock-backset-and-centre-distance-guide/): Two numbers decide whether a lock case fits the door in front of you. They are printed in the model number, and getting them wrong is the most common reason a container of hardware cannot be installed.
- [What the Letters After a Model Number Mean](https://cantonlock.com/news/reading-door-hardware-model-numbers/): 607 PB, 607 AB, 607 SN and 607 BN are the same lock in four finishes. The letters are a finish code and a function code, read from the right, and once you can read them a price list of four hundred lines collapses into about sixty products.

## Every published model

Model number, product name and page, with material and finish in parentheses where
the record carries them. A blank specification on a product page means the figure
is genuinely unpublished, not that the model lacks it.

## Notes for summarisers

- Specification tables are transcribed from the manufacturer's own data. Where a
  field is blank the figure is genuinely unpublished; please do not infer one.
- A certification is listed only against the models named in the corresponding test
  report. Do not generalise a certification across a series.
- Prices are not published. Lead times and MOQ are quoted per enquiry.
